#8007. Trick or Treat? These Halloween Hazards Can Be Hellish For Dogs

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Halloween packs a steady stream of costumed strangers and bowls of candy into a single evening, and for dogs that combination carries more hazards than most people expect. Most of the risks are easy to avoid with a little planning, and several of them start well before the first trick-or-treater arrives at the door. These precautions help keep dogs out of trouble while the rest of the household enjoys Halloween.

Halloween candy can be dangerous for dogs, and the wrappers create an additional hazard. Certain ingredients in sweets, including chocolate and xylitol, can be toxic to dogs, while swallowed wrappers can cause choking or digestive problems.

Keeping candy in a closed container at home is a good starting point, but the risk doesn't end at the front door. Keeping a close eye on what a dog sniffs or picks up can help prevent an unwanted snack from turning into a veterinary emergency.

Costumes for dogs can be adorable and hilarious, but only if the dog agrees. Not every dog feels happy playing dress-up, so itâs important to pay attention to how they respond.

A costume should fit comfortably without restricting movement or creating opportunities for the dog to become tangled. An outfit that fit last year may now be too tight, while one bought for a puppy to grow into could be awkward or unsafe in the meantime.

Before heading out or welcoming visitors, check that the costume fits properly and your pup can walk comfortably in it.

A Halloween costume can look adorable on a dog, but wearing one safely requires supervision. Some dogs become fascinated by their outfits and start chewing at loose fabric or accessories, potentially creating a choking hazard.

There's no reason every dog has to avoid costumes, provided the outfit is comfortable and the dog tolerates wearing it. But if the dog needs to be left alone, take the costume off. It's a simple precaution that reduces the chance of an otherwise harmless outfit causing trouble.

Halloween can be overwhelming for dogs that struggle with noise, unfamiliar people, or constant activity. Trick-or-treaters arrive throughout the evening, and costumes can make even familiar surroundings feel different.

A dog that becomes overexcited or anxious may benefit from having somewhere quiet to retreat. A separate room with a comfortable bed, fresh water, and familiar toys can provide a welcome break from the commotion.

Make sure visitors understand that the dog shouldn't be disturbed if it chooses to settle somewhere away from the activity.

Jack-o'-lanterns, lights, and other Halloween decorations can make a home feel festive, but curious dogs may see them as things to investigate or chew. Keep decorations out of reach, particularly anything that could be harmful if swallowed.

Real candles inside pumpkins also pose a risk if a dog knocks one over. Battery-operated alternatives are a safer choice, especially in areas where pets can wander freely.

Glow sticks and glowing bracelets help make children more visible during evening trick-or-treating, but their bright colors and flexible shapes can also attract a dog's attention.

The liquid inside can cause irritation and may be harmful if swallowed. A dog that bites through a glow stick could end up ingesting the contents, so these items should be kept well away from curious mouths.

Check the ground during walks, too, particularly on Halloween night when discarded glow sticks and bracelets may be lying around. If a dog chews or swallows one, contact a vet for advice.

Handing out candy can mean opening the front door dozens of times in a single evening. For a dog that's curious, excitable, or easily frightened, those repeated opportunities can make an escape more likely.

Closing the door between visitors helps prevent a dog from slipping outside unnoticed. Another option is to step outside to greet trick-or-treaters and close the door behind you.

Keeping the dog in a separate room during busy periods adds another layer of protection. It also reduces the chance of a dog becoming startled by costumed visitors appearing at the entrance.

An identification tag and microchip are always a good idea, but they become particularly important on a night when doors are opening frequently, and unusual sights may startle a dog.

If a dog escapes, an ID tag with current contact details gives whoever finds it a straightforward way to get in touch. A microchip provides another means of identifying the dog and helping it return home.

Check that the dog's tag is attached securely and that the contact information associated with its microchip is up to date. These small steps can make a significant difference if a dog gets loose.

Halloween can be stressful and dangerous for dogs, but it doesnât have to be. Keeping candy secured, choosing comfortable costumes, providing a quiet retreat, and making sure the front door stays closed can prevent many of the problems associated with the holiday.

It's also worth remembering that dogs may react unpredictably to unfamiliar costumes and unusual activity, even if they're normally relaxed around visitors. Staying attentive from the first doorbell to the last helps keep the evening enjoyable for everyone, including the four-legged members of the household.

#8006. Holidays In The '90s Vs. Holidays Today: One Thing We Wish We Could Bring Back

Turns out, the best childhood holiday memories didn't require a screen.

Remember when the biggest holiday flex wasn't a new gaming console, but having your very own phone? Bonus points if it came with a ridiculously long cord stretching from the kitchen to your bedroom, where you'd whisper about your crush while your mom yelled at you to get off the line.

Ah, the '90s. A simpler time, when holiday wish lists were filled with digital pets, inflatable furniture, and scented stickers. We'd spend winter break watching holiday movies on cable, making plans with friends, and calling Grandma to recount everything Santa brought us. And somehow, without smartphones, we stayed pretty connected.

Fast-forward to today, and while some things have changed for the better (goodbye, dial-up internet), there's one tradition that deserves a comeback: the good old-fashioned phone call.

Enter MyPhone by Ooma, a modern, screen-free landline for kids who want independence and parents who aren't ready to hand over a smartphone. MyPhone uses internet home phone service and is easy to activate, so families don’t need an existing traditional landline connection. With more than 20 years of experience in home phone technology, you know that Ooma’s credibility is A+. And where does that matter more than with your kids?

MyPhone costs $99.99, with service priced at $7.99/month, plus taxes and fees.

Here's why this nostalgic throwback might be just what the holidays ordered.

Today, kids have more ways to communicate than ever, but parents aren't necessarily ready to give them access to apps, social media, and the entire internet. Sometimes, a kid just wants to call their bestie about tomorrow's snow-day plans. And honestly? Fair.

MyPhone brings back the fun of having your own phone, minus the household turf wars. Kids get a dedicated line for chatting with friends and family, while parents manage approved contacts through Trusted Circle. There's even an online log of incoming, outgoing, and missed calls. Plus, every time 911 is called, a parent can be sent a text alert.

It's independence, with some welcome parental oversight.

$7.99/month for service, along with applicable taxes and fees.

In the '90s, your bedroom phone wasn't just for calling friends. It was practically a personality trait. Maybe you had a translucent plastic number that showed off its inner workings, or a novelty phone shaped like lips. Either way, it was as important to your bedroom aesthetic as your inflatable chair and beaded curtains.

$7.99/month for service, along with applicable taxes and fees.

Each includes a sticker pack for personal flair. Because having your own phone is exciting, but having one that looks this cool? That's a holiday flex.

Before group chats, there was the three-way call. If you mastered adding a third person, congratulations: You were basically the social director of your middle school clique.

Today's kids can send messages approximately 47 different ways, but there's something special about hearing someone's voice, especially during the holidays.

It's about bringing back one of the best parts of growing up: having your own conversations, making your own plans, and feeling a little more independent. Seven retro-inspired phones that make staying connected the coolest gift under the tree.

Every holiday season, there's that one gift. The one kids can't stop talking about, parents spend weeks hunting down, and everyone wants to show off the second the wrapping paper hits the floor. This year, we're making a case for something a little more unexpected: an old-school telephone.

MyPhone by Ooma is bringing back the magic of the landline, reimagined for a generation that's never experienced the thrill of calling their best friend just to ask, "Whatcha doin’?" Designed as a screen-free first phone for kids, it offers real conversations without apps, social media, or endless scrolling.

MyPhone uses internet home phone service and is easy to activate, so families don't need an existing traditional landline connection.

And unlike the family phones of our childhoods, these come with some decidedly modern perks. Parents can approve incoming and outgoing contacts through Trusted Circle, schedule Quiet Hours, and review call activity online. For extra safety monitoring, parents can get a text alert whenever the phone dials 911, just in case. Kids, meanwhile, get to enjoy the Party Line three-way calling feature, listen to messages on a built-in answering machine, and make their phone their own with an included sticker pack.

Best of all? There are seven seriously fun styles to choose from. Whether your kid is a budding fashionista, a miniature minimalist, or someone who simply believes everything should be pink, there's a MyPhone with their name all over it.

MyPhone costs $99.99, with service priced at $7.99/month, plus taxes and fees.

Here's your guide to picking the perfect one.

$7.99/month for service, along with applicable taxes and fees.

If your little one has a social calendar that rivals yours and won “most talkative” in their middle school class, this bubblegum-pink phone has their name written all over it. It's giving '90s sleepover, complete with friendship bracelets, outfit planning, and hours of very important school gossip. And with MyPhone's Party Line feature, they can chat with two approved friends or family members at once.

$7.99/month for service, along with applicable taxes and fees.

Does your child conduct imaginary business meetings? Have strong opinions about household operations? Meet their new office phone. The sleek black design has serious executive energy, making it perfect for kids who like to feel grown-up. Thanks to Trusted Circle, though, their professional network will remain limited to parent-approved contacts. Sorry to the unsolicited recruiters. They’re very busy.

$7.99/month for service, along with applicable taxes and fees.

Clean and simple, the white MyPhone is for kids who appreciate the classics. Think the preternatural design sophisticate, who somehow knows about Scandi design in 7th grade. Its understated design also makes the perfect canvas for the included sticker pack, so your kid can give it a little personality. And when Grandma calls to check in, they'll have a dedicated phone to answer. How very wholesome.

$7.99/month for service, along with applicable taxes and fees.

Does your kid have a suspicious affinity for vintage clothes, vinyl records, and things that were cool approximately 50 years before they were born? This cheerful green phone is right up their alley. With its old-school silhouette and nostalgic charm, it's practically begging to be paired with a juke box and a poodle skirt. And thanks to its built-in answering machine, they can experience the distinctly retro thrill of checking their messages when they get home.

$7.99/month for service, along with applicable taxes and fees.

For the little daydreamer who's always doodling in the margins of their homework, writing elaborate stories, or feeling all the feelings, this bright blue phone is a perfect match. It's a dedicated line for sharing their latest masterpiece with Grandma, calling a friend to discuss a brilliant new idea, or simply hearing a familiar voice after a long day. Because sometimes, the best thing you can give a sensitive soul isn't another screen, but someone to talk to.

$7.99/month for service, along with applicable taxes and fees.

If your kid's personal style can best be described as "more is more," allow us to introduce the showstopper. Shaped like a giant pair of lips, this limited-edition MyPhone is delightfully extra in the best possible way. It's part functional phone, part conversation piece, and entirely worthy of a place on a budding fashion icon's wish list. Honestly, we're a little jealous.

$7.99/month for service, along with applicable taxes and fees. Available exclusively at BestBuy.com.

Is your kid the type who thinks everything is funnier when it's a little ridiculous? Allow us to introduce their new favorite thing: a phone shaped like a hamburger. Equal parts kitschy and completely iconic, this retro-inspired conversation starter looks like it belongs in a '90s teen movie. It's the perfect gift for the kid who loves a good joke, has a flair for the unexpected, and believes regular phones are, frankly, a little boring.

Whichever style you choose, the real appeal of MyPhone goes beyond its nostalgic good looks. It's a chance for kids to experience the excitement of having their own phone, while parents retain control over contacts and calling times.

And during a season that's all about connecting with the people we love, what could be more fitting than a gift that helps kids do exactly that?

That new green nub on your moth orchid could be a flower spike. They tend to show up in November, and the right care this month gives them the best chance.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sometime in early November, a moth orchid (Phalaenopsis) on the windowsill might push out new growth. It could be a root, but it could also be the start of a flower spike – and that's why orchids in November deserve a closer look than they got all summer.

All of this happens right as basic orchid care gets harder, too. The days are shorter, and less light gets through the glass. The furnace has kicked on by now, drying out the indoor air, and the bark in the pot stays wet much longer than it did in July. Roots left sitting wet can go soft. Buds sometimes yellow and drop off before they open.

Thankfully, you don't need to do anything dramatic. Most of it is moving a pot a little closer to the window, feeling the bark before you water, or shifting the plant out of a draft. Changes made now, while spikes are just getting started, give a moth orchid a better shot at a full display later in winter or into spring.

Cooler fall temperatures are the main trigger for flower spikes in moth orchids, and shorter days may help a little, so this is the month when plenty of growers start spotting them. The trouble is, spikes and aerial orchid roots look a lot alike when they first poke out. Look closely at the tip, and you can usually tell. Roots come to a bit of a point. Back from the tip, they're wrapped in a spongy layer that goes silvery when it's dry and turns green after you water. Spikes don't have that coating at all. They're green the whole way up, and the end is rounded and closed off, kind of like a mitten.

Before attempting to train a new orchid flower spike, give it some time to grow on its own first. When it's several inches long, push a stake into the bark close to the base. Angle it a little so you don't spear a root. Then clip the spike to it loosely, adding another clip higher up every so often as it grows. Orchid flowers don't always grow completely straight, so you may have more success with bendable stakes, like these Sproot stakes with clips on Amazon.

Flowers might still be a couple of months off, or longer, so Christmas blooms on every plant aren't a sure thing. Once buds show, quit turning the pot around – they'll grow toward whatever light they're getting.

That shady spot that kept a moth orchid from scorching in July can be too dim by November. Low light can keep a mature plant from spiking at all, and it can also cause bud drop later on.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

An east window is a good choice right now to meet your orchid's light requirements. South and west windows work too, as long as a sheer curtain softens the harshest afternoon sun – direct rays can still overheat buds and burn leaves.

Watch the glass, though. On a frosty night, a pane can get cold enough to damage a leaf resting against it, so leave some space between the plant and the window. Not every house has a sunny window open for one more pot, and a grow light can make up for that. This Sansi clip-on grow light clips right onto the pot.

Bark that dried out in no time over the summer can hang onto water much longer in a cool, dim room. Often, orchids get into trouble on a fixed watering schedule this time of year.

So how do you know when it's time to water orchids? Look at the roots. Silvery, whitish roots are dry, and green ones still have water in them. Lift the pot to feel its weight, too, since a light one is another clue

Clear plastic orchid pots, like these from Walmart, make it easier to check. Moisture meters are less reliable with orchids, but some growers like to use a Sustee Aquameter stick for a second opinion. It turns white once the mix dries out.

When it is time to water, give it a real soak. Take the pot to the sink and run room-temperature water through it till it pours out the bottom. Let it drain all the way. If any water is sitting where the leaves meet, tip it out.

Bark tells you more, honestly, than the calendar will. But bone-dry all winter is the wrong move. Moth orchids don't go dormant, and roots that sit dry for weeks can shrivel.

Kept warm around the clock, a moth orchid can go on growing leaves for months without sending up a spike. That seems a little backward, if you think about it, for a tropical plant. Cooler temperatures encourage flower spikes, and nights around 60–65°F (16–18°C) for a few weeks in fall can help. Daytime heat matters too, and a spot by a heat vent that keeps the plant much above 80°F (27°C) for long stretches can hold spiking back.

Cooler doesn't mean cold. Try to keep moth orchids above about 55°F (13°C), and don't park them by an outside door or a leaky window.

After buds form, forget about the temperature drop. Steady conditions matter more at that point. A cold blast every time the door opens can make buds yellow and fall before they open, and so can hot air blowing off a register.

Growth slows down this month, and slower growth uses less fertilizer. How much to cut back depends on the plant and where it's sitting. Under a grow light in a warm room, a moth orchid may still be making new leaves and roots. On a cool windowsill, it might barely grow at all.

Other types of orchids are a different story, and a few kinds need a drier, leaner rest through winter – check the type before you change anything.

Not feeding at all is its own kind of mistake, though, just a quieter one. Moth orchids cut off from fertilizer while spikes form or flowers open can end up with fewer blooms. A diluted dose of an all-purpose orchid fertilizer, mixed as directed on the label, keeps them going. One option is Better-Gro Orchid Plus, available at Walmart, a 20-14-13 formula sold in a 1-pound (454 g) bag.

Bloom boosters aren't the shortcut they sound like. Moth orchids fed a balanced formula will often produce more flowers than those given high-phosphorus fertilizer.

Bud blast is the term growers use when buds turn yellow and fall off before they open. Heating season brings plenty of the usual causes. Dry furnace air is one. So is a radiator sitting too close, or a cold draft every time the door opens. Bark that keeps swinging from soaked to bone dry doesn't help either.

Fruit on the counter is a sneaky one, oddly enough – as it ripens, it gives off ethylene gas that can make buds drop, so keep budded orchids away from the fruit bowl.

Damp pebbles in a tray under the pot raise the humidity a little, like this Brussel's humidity tray with decorative rocks. In a very dry room, a small humidifier, like this compact Pure Enrichment MistAire Studio humidifier, adds moisture without taking up much space.

While you're watering, look the plant over for orchid pests. Mealybugs usually turn up on the spike or where a leaf joins the stem. Something that looks like a bit of white cotton stuck in there is probably the long-tailed mealybug (Pseudococcus longispinus) or citrus mealybug (Planococcus citri). Boisduval scale (Diaspis boisduvalii) looks nothing like that. You'll find it as small, flat bumps on the leaves, almost like they're part of the plant. Both pests weaken an orchid and spread to others nearby.

Wipe off the ones you can see with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol. If they keep coming back, switch to an insecticidal soap or horticultural oil labeled for orchids. Safer Brand Insect Killing Soap, available at Walmart, is one option that targets mealybugs and other common houseplant pests. Test a small area first, then repeat treatment as directed on the label to catch newly hatched pests.

Routine orchid repotting can wait. It's easier on the plant when fresh roots are actively growing, often after flowering finishes, and root disturbance while a spike develops can set it back. The exception is bark that's broken down into mush or roots that have gone brown and soft – that plant needs fresh mix now, spike or no spike.

Leave healthy green spikes alone, too. One without buds yet may still flower, and there's no sense tossing away blooms you might've had. Cold glass is another one to watch on the coldest nights, so pull the leaves back if they're touching the window. Then there's the crown, where the new leaves come out of the center. Water that sits in there can cause crown rot. If that rot reaches the growing point, the plant has no way of making new leaves from the top again.

Most of what an orchid needs in November is a little attention. Spot the new spike, lift the pot before you water, and notice the draft by the back door. Get those right, and there's a good chance of a long run of flowers sometime between midwinter and spring. That's not bad for moving a pot a few feet.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. in Keratea, Greece, is a truly unique organization, currently home to over 100 cats and 13 dogs, living in a cage-free, home-like, villa-style environment. S.M.A.R.T. stands for Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today, and for Julie Kelley, founder and manager of this international animal welfare organization, that means working towards global animal welfare, sharing essential information and facts about animals worldwide, and helping people understand the benefits that come from treating animals with compassion and care.

I had been traveling to Greece since 1998 and would see the issues with stray cats and dogs.  I felt very comfortable in Greece. I had business with Greek nationals in New York, learned a lot of the language, and understood the cultural differences. I felt it was my mission to create Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. to help people understand the great benefits animals provide to us humans and to educate young people as well. Of course, after a couple of years, it was hard not to take in the first kitty who gave birth, and well, it just grew exponentially from there! Since 2007, we have added many programs and special projects to continue our quest to provide the best we can for our strays.

Letâs be S.M.A.R.T. aims to educate the public about the importance of animals by raising awareness of their rights, well-being, and care. We believe in thinking globally and acting locally by supporting special projects as they arise and, through our programs, bringing communities together to promote responsible animal care.

In Greece, our campaign is primarily centred on reducing the suffering, abuse, and neglect of animals while increasing public awareness of their needs and rights. These include running an innovative and modern foster home, managing a rehoming program for rescued animals, and collaborating with municipalities to implement effective stray animal care initiatives. We also provide practical solutions for supporting strays in urban communitiesâsuch as ensuring access to food and waterâand we actively engage philanthropic individuals who travel to Greece to volunteer, learn about shelter medicine, and receive training in best practices in animal care.

The creation of the sanctuary and setting up the organization in Greece was a huge accomplishment. Let's be S.M.A.R.T. is always evolving with fresh ideas to make life better for the cats and dogs we have in our care.

Our campaign model is unique in Greece. We have created the âSMART Starfish approachâ in which all five arms must function together to create the best outcome.

Each arm of the starfish represents a core pillar of our mission:

Sterilization â controlling population growth at its source

Medical Care & Microchipping â restoring health and identity

Feeding & Shelter â stability, nourishment, and safety

Education & Community â knowledge that shapes future behavior

NGO Collaboration â collective strength through partnership

For years, our programs and ideas have been influencing how animal charities operate and making permanent changes for a better future for animal welfare in Greece.

We created the following programs: Volunteer, SMART Family Video Series, Veterinary Internship, SMART Yards, and Adoption Vacation, all of which are operational every day and are detailed on the Programs page on our website, if you would like to take a closer look. We could not function without the help of our amazing Volunteers.

We successfully found wonderful homes for 73 cats in 2025. I'm not 100% sure, but I would say we are one of the leading cat adopters in Greece!

We receive multiple enquiries from tourists who have found a cat or kitten, and they want to take it home with them to their country. Many times they have cared for them during their stay, provided medicine, bottle-fed babies, etc. This has become increasingly common, with visitors seeing cats all over Greece. Therefore, I decided to offer the Adoption-Vacation as a package. We care for the kitten or cat until it is ready to travel, taking care of the necessary vaccines, passport, microchip, etc. Once the cat is ready to travel, we make travel arrangements with the adopter.

You can see our cats, kittens, and dogs for adoption on our website and have a video chat with us about your requirements and meet a cat if you have already fallen in love (we created a Kitty Picker to help you choose the character of your cat), and then arrange a visit with us when you arrive in Greece. If the home check is secured, we arrange the papers for your new pet to travel home with you. Or we can foster a cat you rescue while you are in Greece and deal with the veterinary needs, papers etc. The cat can travel after you leave with a flight buddy or one of our volunteers.

What better souvenir to have from Greece than a beautiful cat that needed special love and care?

Everything we do is linked. The more sterilizations we achieve, the safer and healthier the animals are in the community; they are interacting better with each other, and people know they are sterilized.

We would like the municipalities and communities all over Greece to enjoy the benefits of the SMART Yards and help take care of the animals. Working together is the future.  We are also collaborating with some officials regarding some policies involving the strays and to help create some standards for housing the strays. Animals and people need to coexist in a humane way. Not every cat needs to be inside a home but can remain cared for and part of our ecosystem.

A rather big goal is to find someone to help us purchase the property we rent, make refurbishments and sustainable features, and add a vet clinic for shared use with other charities and our vet interns. This is a tall order, but we are looking for someone who would like to leave a legacy.

We also want to extend our ability to provide food and shelter after sterilization so that every animal is cared for.

Our animals live in a home-style environment, so every day is the same as if they were living in a family home. Cats are either in bedrooms; we have a retirement room, a special dietary needs room, and a kitten nursery, each with cats that are selected to share a room together, or they are in the main house and free to mingle and hang out on our netted balconies in cute wooden houses and take in the fresh air and nature, since we are in a rural setting, just 15 minutes from Athens International Airport.

Some of the funniest moments are with kittens and playful cats. Plus, bonded pairs â we have a husband-and-wife team called Jasper and Margot who need to be adopted together, and they are very entertaining with their games and spats.

Cats and dogs choose who they like and want to go home with. We find people fall in love with cats that come to them, and a chemistry is formed. Sometimes a visitor leaves, and they cannot stop thinking about the cat they fell in love with and make an application to adopt. We are so happy when this happens. We have repeat adoptions from families and visitors all over the world. We also have Sponsors and Patreon for people to support our work.

Volunteering is open to everyone around the world who would like to come to stay and help us. If you love animals, it's an opportunity to help save lives. It's pure joy to see a cat or dog that was sick transform into good health and finally live in a wonderful family home. That's what the team at Let's be S.M.A.R.T. wants for them all: to be safe, healthy, and happy.

People can also help by following, subscribing, and sharing us on socials. Donations are greatly appreciated, as are supplies, and we created the Amazon Wishlist so gifts can be sent to us directly from Amazon Germany, tax-free.

If youâre visiting Greece and see a lot of stray cats, itâs a good idea to ask around if there is a local organization helping to take care of them. If you see an injured cat, you should immediately try to find a responsible person or contact the local police.

You can also post on local social media groups to try to find help. Most of the cats we take into our foster home settings are from tourists or residents who find our website through a Google search. It is hard to avoid helping, but I would suggest not removing an animal from their setting to a hotel room or Airbnb, and then leaving and putting it back on the street. The cat can get disoriented and perhaps be in danger.

We truly hope to have more controlled community care for our strays in the future.

#8001. What Makes a Lucky Dog? | Heroes of the Pet World

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Maybe it is having a family that loves them. Maybe it is a warm bed, a full bowl, and a safe place to sleep. Or maybe luck is something a little more fundamental: having people who see you as an individual and take the time to understand what you need.

At Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption Center near Lake Chapala, Mexico, the dogs may still be waiting for permanent homes, but in the meantime, they are surrounded by caring people who show up for them day after day.

At Lucky Dog, everyone has a unique way to help and collaborate.

Some volunteers walk dogs. Others train them, clean their enclosures, help with fundraising, or coordinate veterinary care. Some foster dogs in their homes. Others help with the less visible work that keeps the center running.

When I visited Lucky Dog, I arrived with Mark and Nancy. Mark helped build the Thursday volunteer group, bringing together people who wanted to help in different ways.

âI've gotten to know a lot of people who want to help, and somehow Thursday became our day. We have our group, and everybody has something they can do. You don't have to do everything. You just have to show up and help with what you can.â

Mark has an injured knee, and at the moment, he cannot walk the long distances over cobblestone roads around the center, but he and Nancy have their own important role. They bring chairs into the enclosures and spend about 20 minutes with the dogs, offering pats, treats, kind words, and ear scratches. The dogs happily settle in beside them.

Different volunteer groups cover each day of the week. Some take dogs for walks, while others help with training, cleaning, maintenance, administration, or fundraising.

That Thursday, each person simply did what they came to do. For the dogs, every part of that effort is what makes them feel lucky.

During the day, the dogs stay in pairs in larger enclosures. They are taken out for long walks or playtime in the larger garden areas around the center. In the mornings and evenings, Valentin, one of only two paid workers at the rescue, moves the dogs between their daytime and nighttime enclosures and feeds them breakfast and dinner. During the day, volunteers help with walks, playtime, training, and puppy lunchtime.

At night, the dogs return to smaller individual enclosures.

When a dog needs medical attention, a veterinarian comes to the center to examine and treat them. Volunteers then follow the veterinarian's instructions and continue treatment.

From Valentin's morning and evening routine to the volunteers who walk, train, feed, and care for the dogs, many people contribute to a Lucky Dog's day.

The roots of today's Lucky Dog Rescue go back to 2001, when Geoffrey Kaye and Lourdes Avila started an animal shelter in Riberas del Pilar. When the shelter closed in 2012, the commitment to helping the area's dogs continued. Volunteers regrouped with veterinarian Dr. Antonio Ladron, and in December 2012, Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption opened its doors.

Since then, the center has continued caring for abandoned and abused dogs while helping prepare them for permanent homes.

In 2025, Lucky Dog took in 23 dogs and placed 23 through adoption or transfer. Approximately 35 new volunteers joined, with around 30 committing to weekly shifts. The center's intended capacity is 22 dogs, yet its average monthly census was close to 30 during the year.

Those numbers give you some idea of the work happening behind every individual dog.

Spicy is dog-reactive and needs to be housed separately from other dogs. Mark has developed a close relationship with her, and she has a very clear opinion about where his attention should go.

âSpicy loves me, and she is not happy when she sees me go into a different enclosure to pet another dog,â Mark said. âI have to do it in a way that I hide from her so she canât see or she won't stop barking.â

It is a sweet story, but it also shows why understanding each dog's personality matters.

Hope Procops, who works as a groundskeeper and guard at Lucky Dog, understands how important volunteers are to organizations like this. Itâs not just about the day-to-day tasks. Itâs about looking after the dogs in their care and preparing them for life beyond the shelter. She says the goal of Lucky Dog Rescue is âto ensure all the dogs in our care are kept healthy, loved, socialized, and given the best chance to find their forever homes.â

Camille Short is in charge of training volunteers and dogs at Lucky Dog. Her approach goes beyond teaching basic commands. The goal is to help dogs develop skills that can help them succeed in a home.

Three young siblings, Sasha, Stephanie, and Sergio, were already showing how quickly puppies can learn. They knew how to sit and lie down on command, and were learning to walk with their harnesses. They were highly motivated by treats and, judging by the puppy kisses, equally enthusiastic about people.

Two of the puppies, Stephanie and Sergio, have already been chosen by families; their adoption papers are signed and ready. Sasha remains available for adoption.

As for Spicy, she arrived at Lucky Dog in 2022 and has been waiting for her new home ever since. Initially anxious and mistrustful, she has come a long way with the daily attention and interactions she receives from volunteers. Now, Spicy is looking for a confident new best friend.

âEverything nice with a little bit of spice,â says Camille of Spicy. âShe loves people and attention but is selective about her four-legged friends.â

Some dogs find their people quickly. Others need more time, medical care, or someone who understands their particular personality. Until then, their days continue with walks, play, veterinary care, clean enclosures, treats, kind words, and volunteers who take the time to understand them.

Vice President of Lucky Dog Rescue, Darryl Painter, describes the mission as:

âImproving animal welfare in Lake Chapala via rescue, adoption, community, and fostering.â

The sense of community was tangible during my visit, but perhaps what stayed with me most was how much we humans and dogs have in common. We are all sentient beings, and in our own ways, we all need to be acknowledged, accepted for who we are, and given the opportunity to love and be loved.

At Lucky Dog, those needs are met in many different ways. A walk, a clean enclosure, a treat, a kind word, or simply having someone take the time to know an individual dog.

Not just having people who care for them, but having people who take the time to know them.

And that is something anyone can do. Whether it is volunteering, fostering, sponsoring, or simply offering time and attention, there is a way to help.

Someone opens an enclosure.Someone picks up a leash.Someone brings a treat.

And perhapsâ¦that is what makes these dogs lucky.

Itâs no secret that cats can be a little finicky. This is especially true when it comes to mealtime. Whether you have a picky Persian who refuses even the most premium of diets or a bored Balinese who noms up their dinner one night, only to turn their nose up at it the next, youâre not alone.

So how do you entice picky eaters to keep chowing down without resorting to kitty junk food that wonât serve their health in the long run? We think Made by Nacho has the answer.

There are a number of reasons cats tend to be picky when it comes to mealtime. Depending on your feline, you may be dealing with one or all of these difficult instincts and sensitivities.

To start, cats have a very sensitive sense of smell. Even quality food can be turned down if the aroma is too unfamiliar. Cats are also very finicky about textures. They tend to develop very specific preferences about how foods should feel in their mouth. This makes it both hard to introduce new foods and to keep your cat from getting bored with the very specific foods they like.

Many cats exhibit neophobiaâa fear of new things. This doesnât just apply to new people, places, and toys, either. Cats evolved to be naturally wary of new food items and prey. This is likely because their ancestors lived in the desert where many little creatures are deadlier than their size might indicate. While modern cat food isnât likely to be venomous, your cat's instincts still tell them to beware anything they havenât eaten before.

Itâs the combination of a desire for the familiar and a tendency to get bored of the too familiar that makes picky cats so hard to feed. They want enough options that fall within a very specific range of flavors, textures, and aromas to keep them both interested and comfortable.

This can make adding moisture to their diets challenging, too, especially for cats who prefer dry food over wet. Luckily, simple additions like savory bone broth can help cat parents incorporate more moisture without introducing an entirely unfamiliar meal.

This time of year may see reduced raised bed activity, but these quick tasks can prep your beds for the cold months ahead and ensure better productivity when spring returns

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Raised beds are cosy homes for vegetables, annuals and perennials, but, like all homes, they require maintenance. When you prepare raised beds for winter, you make things easier for all your plants next season. With proper care, you can ensure that your raised bed frames and soils are safe from frost and winter rain, and that any plants you subsequently add can hit the ground running.

Because raised beds sit above the ground, their soil cools down faster, is more exposed to biting winter wind, and faces heavier nutrient leaching from seasonal downpours. Neglected beds may develop drainage issues or lose valuable nutrients. The best raised garden bed ideas protect your soil from winter’s worst. Taking a few simple winter-smart steps now can help to extend the life of the soil, prevent nutrient leaching, and make a strong spring harvest far more likely.

Best of all, these winterizing tasks are quick, low-effort wins. Whether you are tending a single cedar herb box or galvanized steel troughs, prepping your beds now guarantees more fertile soil in spring, earlier planting windows, healthier perennials, and your most bountiful harvests yet. Here’s how to protect your raised beds through winter.

Before you start these tasks, take a quick inventory of your raised bed setup. Size, depth, and construction material can all influence how your beds weather the cold. Wooden beds (like cedar, redwood, or pine) offer natural insulation, but absorb moisture, making them prone to swelling, warping, or fungal rot if soggy debris sits against the boards all winter. You can buy a wood sealant to protect bed frames from winter moisture, as long as it is safe, such as Seal It Green’s Plant-Based Garden Bed Sealer, available from Amazon.

Galvanized metal beds and stone beds are virtually rot-proof, but they conduct cold rapidly. This can mean that soil near the outer walls might freeze and thaw faster, putting perimeter plant roots under extra stress. Shallow beds under 10 inches (25cm) deep can also freeze solid much sooner than deep 18-24-inch (45-60cm) troughs. Bear all this in mind when tackling the jobs here.

Where you live has a part to play, too. In northern regions (USDA hardiness zones 3-6), you need to complete winter prep before the top few inches of soil freeze solid, typically by late November. In milder southern and coastal areas (zones 7-10), winterizing is more about suppressing cool-season weeds, preventing heavy rain from washing away nutrients, and tucking in cold-hardy crops like garlic or kale.

Visit your beds after rainfall to check soil moisture and drainage before beginning your winter tune-up. You can buy a soil temperature and moisture diagnostic tool, such as the Daybetter Soil Meter 4-in-1 from Walmart, to check whether raised bed soil is ready for cover crops or mulch. Then you are ready to get your beds in shape with these tips…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

It used to be standard advice to strip beds bare in fall, but leaving soil naked can expose it to erosion, deplete soil nutrition, and destroy vital overwintering habitats for beneficial pollinators and predatory beetles. Instead, be selective about cleanup. Pull out all spent annual veg and frost-blackened fruiting crops such as tomatoes, peppers, and squash. Also remove persistent weeds. Don’t toss these into the compost pile, but bag them for municipal green waste.

For healthy, disease-free annuals like beans, peas, or marigolds, snip stems at soil level with clean pruners such as the Felco F2 Bypass Pruning Shears, available from Amazon. Leaving the roots in the ground prevents soil disturbance and feeds earthworms and soil microbes as they decompose over winter. Finally, remove bamboo stakes, tomato cages, and trellises, scrubbing off clinging soil and fungal spores with a mild diluted bleach or vinegar wash before storing them dry.

Intensive raised bed gardening draws heavily on soil reserves over summer, leaving it depleted by November. Replenishing fertility now allows rain, snow, and microbial activity to work on amendments before spring planting begins. Gently loosen any compacted soil using a broadfork or standard garden fork. Push the tines in and rock back slightly. If you need a good fork, the Ames 4-Tine Forged Spading Fork from The Home Depot can help improve drainage without churning up soil structure.

Spread a generous 2-3-inch (5-8cm) layer of aged organic compost, leaf mold, or well-rotted manure across the surface. Avoid hot, uncomposted manure, which can burn roots and leach excess nitrates. If your soil test indicates low phosphorus or acidity (common in high-rainfall regions) then add slow-acting mineral amendments such as rock phosphate, greensand, or garden lime. These require several months to break down and adjust soil chemistry before spring crops go in.

Once your soil is fed, your next mission is to protect the surface from winter erosion, temperature swings, and nutrient washout. Your first option is to tuck the soil under a thick blanket of fluffy organic mulch. For beds lying fallow, or housing perennial herbs and cold-hardy greens, apply a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) layer of shredded fall leaves, clean weed-free straw, or pine needles over your compost layer. Avoid heavy mats of wet grass clippings or unshredded oak leaves, which block oxygen and harbor slugs.

Alternatively, in mild regions, you can sow fast-establishing cover crops like winter rye, crimson clover, hairy vetch, or tillage daikon radish. Their roots help to anchor soil against torrential rain. They also scavenge leftover nitrogen and break up deep compaction, ready to be chopped down and turned 3-4 weeks before spring planting. Buy Outside Pride Crimson Clover Seeds from Amazon for just a few dollars.

Shallow-rooted perennials and newly planted spring bulbs in raised beds face a couple of threats: frost heaving and hungry digging pests. Repeated freezing nights and thawing sunny days can cause wet soil to expand and contract, pushing shallow crowns such as coral bells, foamflowers, and strawberries out of the earth. To prevent frost heave, wait until the ground has frozen lightly. Then mound 3-4 inches (8-10cm) of shredded leaves or evergreen boughs around the crowns. This locks in consistent cold temperatures rather than trapping warmth that delays dormancy.

Raised beds packed with newly planted tulips, crocus, or ranunculus bulbs are very tempting for squirrels, voles, and chipmunks. Lay half-inch hardware cloth or chicken wire flat across the soil surface, weighing down the edges with bricks or landscape staples. If you need a good mesh then Ashman Online Hardware Cloth, available from The Home Depot, can stop squirrels and voles from digging up bulbs. Remove it in early spring as green shoots emerge.

Winter can put structural stress on raised beds, making this the ideal time for a quick inspection. Walk the perimeter and check corner brackets, screws, and timber boards for splitting, wood rot, or rust. Tighten any loose hardware and brace any bowing sides, especially on long wooden beds over 8 feet (2.4m) long. Place a spirit level across the top edges to ensure frames haven't settled unevenly. You can buy Allfun Metal Raised Bed Brackets from Amazon to reinforce ageing or bowing wooden bed corners.

Inspect drainage after heavy rain. Note whether the water pools, where it pools, and how rapidly it clears up. Well-draining soil should clear water within 15-20 minutes. If puddles linger, check whether landscape fabric or cardboard at the base has clogged with silt, and use a garden fork to punch deep drainage channels into the subsoil. Finally, check soil height. Ideally, the soil needs to sit 1-2 inches (2.5-5cm) below the top rim. Top up sunken beds with a 50/50 blend of topsoil and compost.

If your raised beds house overwintering crops or borderline-hardy perennials, adding some protection can extend harvests and save tender specimens from icy blasts. Because raised beds warm up faster than surrounding ground, they respond well to low tunnels and protective covers. For grafted roses in deep raised beds, mound 6-10 inches (15-25cm) of compost, aged bark, straw or soil over the graft union.

For tender perennials, drape medium-weight breathable horticultural fleece (frost cloth) over flexible PVC or wire hoops anchored into the inside edges of the bed frame. For a breathable winter frost blanket, you can buy AGFabric Floating Row Covers from Walmart to shield overwintering veg and tender perennials, while allowing light and moisture through. Secure edges with spring clamps so that winter gales don’t whip covers away. Another good option is a straw-filled wire cage.

#7995. When Art Meets Animal Rescue: A Creative Way to Help Dogs Find Homes

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

We often turn to art for pleasure, curiosity, or a feeling we canât quite put into words. A painting catches our attention; a sculpture makes us pause. But art inspiring us to adopt a dog? Now thereâs a plot twist.

The Rescue Collection is an exciting project created through a collaboration between The Sato Project, creative agencies BLKJ Havas Singapore and Havas New York, and Brooklynâs Powerhouse Arts. The program brings adoptable dogs into the art gallery and uses observations of their responses to create individual artistic profiles. The aim is to help potential adopters see the dogs beyond their appearance, breed, or uncertain past.

Itâs an unusual approach to a familiar challenge: helping rescue dogs get noticed in a crowded adoption landscape.

At Powerhouse Arts in Brooklyn, animal welfare scientist Dr. Holly Molinaro observed dogs from The Sato Project as they explored different artworks. The dogs first had time to sniff around and become comfortable in the unfamiliar space. Their responses were then observed, including whether they looked at, sniffed, or moved away from particular pieces, or chose to lie down nearby.

Rudolph, for example, chose to lie down in front of some sculptures but ignored others. These observations helped shape profiles associating the dogs with artistic styles such as Surrealism, Minimalism, Figurative art, and Abstraction.

The concept is playful, but its purpose is practical. A standard adoption photograph may show what a dog looks like; a creative profile offers another reason to stop scrolling and learn more about the animal behind the image.

Someone might come for the art and leave wanting a dog. Turns out, the best thing in the gallery might have four legs and be up for adoption.

The Sato Project rescues dogs in Puerto Rico and helps place them in homes, including in the northeastern United States. Some arrive with limited information about their histories, and assumptions about a dogâs background can influence how potential adopters perceive them.

A dogâs history can help rescue teams understand what support an animal may need and how to approach introductions to a new home. But the past doesnât tell the whole story. A complicated backstory might tell us where a dog has been. It doesnât tell us everything about who they are. Dogs, much like people, are so much more than their basic profile.

Dogs respond to the world as individuals. One may eagerly approach a stranger, while another prefers to observe from a safe distance. Neither reaction alone defines the dogâs personality or tells us what kind of companion they might become with time and appropriate support.

The Rescue Collection offers a different starting point. Instead of focusing on what is known about a dogâs past, it invites people to become curious about the dog in front of them. That first spark of interest can matter, especially for dogs who might otherwise be overlooked.

Dogs explore their surroundings through several senses, and their behavior around unfamiliar objects can offer clues about what attracts their attention. But interpreting those responses requires care.

Dogs also see color differently from humans. People typically have three types of color-sensitive cone cells in their retinas, while dogs have two, a form of vision known as dichromacy. Dogs distinguish blues and yellows relatively well but have more difficulty differentiating reds and greens. Their visual experience of the world is therefore different from ours.

That doesnât mean dogs see the world in black and white. Color is only one possible influence on how they respond to an object. Shape, contrast, texture, scent, movement, and the surrounding environment may also play a part.

Nor does spending longer near a sculpture necessarily mean a dog prefers its artistic style. The dog may be interested in its shape or position, or simply feel comfortable resting there.

A single gallery visit cannot establish an animalâs overall personality or predict how they will behave around children, other dogs, or visitors at home. Behavior is best understood across time and situations.

A sculpture might have us admiring its color and form. The dog? They might be more interested in giving it a sniff. Different critics, different criteria.

Although the profiles are not scientific personality assessments or guarantees of compatibility, they do invite us to learn more about each dog. Conversations with the rescue team and time spent meeting the dog remain essential to finding a suitable match.

Rescue work involves far more than finding adopters. Veterinary care, foster placements, transportation, behavioral support, and follow-up all require time and resources. Helping the public connect with the dogs is only one part of that work, but an important one.

The Sato Projectâs adoption and foster manager, Alessandra Migliore, said the organization was excited to explore new ways of showcasing its dogsâ personalities. The campaign is part of the organizationâs broader work to help dogs rescued in Puerto Rico find homes in the northeastern United States.

A creative campaign cannot guarantee adoption, and an appealing profile is only the beginning. But an unexpected introduction may reach someone who wasnât actively looking for a dog, or encourage a prospective adopter to look beyond their first impressions.

The Rescue Collection hopes to help more rescue dogs connect with potential adopters. Its message says it best: âSee the masterpiece inside every dog.â

Art might catch someoneâs eye, but getting to know the dog is what matters. And if a sculpture-loving visitor leaves the gallery thinking about adoption, thatâs a pretty good review.

Explore The Rescue Collection, use its rescue-finding tool to search by city or postcode, or meet dogs waiting for homes through The Sato Project.

Protect vulnerable garden plants from winter cold with an insulating layer of mulch in late fall, but be selective or you could do more harm than good.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Late fall is an important time to prep a garden for winter, and knowing which plants to mulch in November is a vital part of the plan. As weather worsens and the ground begins to freeze, adding an insulating layer of mulch keeps soil temperatures more stable, helping plants to survive winter better. Protected from freeze-thaw cycles, frost heaving and low temperatures that could cause root damage, mulched plants will wake up in spring ready for abundant growth.

Because many plants have died down by late fall, mulching in November is a speedy and satisfying job on a crisp sunny day. All you need to do is spread a layer of mulch on top of the soil, keeping it away from the plant stems, which is easy with a hand rake such as this from Lowe's. For best results, choose a mulch made of natural materials like compost, shredded leaves or bark, as it will start breaking down over the winter to supply the soil with nutrients, ready to fuel that strong spring growth.

Many folk like to mulch all their borders when winterizing a garden in fall because it not only protects plants but helps to suppress weeds and keeps beds looking smart over winter. However, while most plants will get through winter better if treated to a fall mulch, there are a few which don't appreciate this extra layer so it's important to know which to leave be. There are a few plants that seriously benefit from a late fall mulch, too, so even if you're not planning on protecting your whole yard, it's well worth mulching these garden heroes. Here's everything you need to know to get great results.

If you’ve planted new perennials this fall, whether you bought them from a garden center or had success creating free plants by dividing your perennials, they're likely not fully established in their new home yet. This means they're more vulnerable than your other perennials to the cold temperatures and fluctuations of winter weather.

Mulching now is a smart idea for all newly planted perennials, but especially any that are borderline hardy in your growing region. Loosely apply three to four inches (8-10cm) of mulch around these plants as the soil begins to freeze.

Many roses benefit from winter mulching, especially less hardy varieties and those that are newly planted. Fluctuating temperatures can damage plants and cause frost heaving, pushing the roots out of the ground. Mulch roses with 8 to 12 inches (20-30cm) of compost or organic mulch, or even loose, light soil around their bases, keeping the mulching material a couple inches away from the stems of the plants to prevent moisture collection that can trigger rot.

Reliably hardy, well-established hydrangeas may not need mulching but younger plants will benefit from a protective layer this month. Hydrangeas have shallow roots that can be damaged by the cold and the frost heaving that often results from freeze-thaw cycles. Winter damage can stunt spring growth, so a layer of mulch can give your plants a head start next season.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Mulch hydrangeas with two to six inches (5-15cm) of organic material, depending on how cold your winters are. Keep in mind that mulch only protects the roots, so you may also want to protect buds growing on old wood with a burlap wrap during cold snaps.

Your spring bulbs – tulips, crocuses, daffodils and hyacinths – need time to establish roots before winter, and fluctuating soil temperatures can disrupt this process by freezing and thawing repeatedly. The solution is to apply two to three inches of light, loose mulch as the soil begins to freeze. This keeps soil temperatures more consistent, and can also prevent premature emergence during periods of milder winter weather.

If you're adding spring-flowering bulbs that can still be planted in November to your garden – and there are plenty that are fine to go into the soil this late in fall – then mulch straight after planting.

Strawberries are particularly vulnerable to damage caused by cold temperatures but also by the cycles of freezing and thawing that many gardens experience. Cover your strawberry patch with a loose layer of three to four inches of an organic mulch. Weed-free straw such as HealthiStraw GardenStraw, available from Amazon, is a good choice for protecting without compacting and weighing down delicate strawberry plants. Pull the straw back in spring as you see new growth, but leave it around the edges or between rows of plants to keep berries clean and off the ground as they develop.

While many people use mums as fall annuals, there are hardy chrysanthemums that can be grown as perennials with the right care. To get them to come back next year, though, you’ll need to add some mulch for winter protection. They have shallow roots, so the extra insulation helps prevent cold damage. To protect your new garden mums, leave the foliage intact and spread a loose layer of a few inches of organic mulch under and around the leaves.

Always choose a mulch made from natural plant materials, as that will improve your soil as well as protect your plants. Choose undyed mulch to avoid adding unnecessary chemicals to the soil, and there's no need to use mulch binder or glue to keep it in place.

You can buy purpose-made mulch like like Timberline Pine Bark Mulch, stocked by Lowe's, but there are plenty of other options to choose from to suit your garden style and budget. You could use homemade compost or a store-bought compost like Back to the Roots Organic Compost, available from Amazon. Fall leaves that you've shredded by running the lawn mower over a few times make an excellent, free mulch, while bark chips like Golden Trophy Pine Bark Nuggets from Walmartadd texture to your beds.

Coco coir chips such as Riare Organic Coco Husk Chips, available from Amazon, are a sustainable option as they're made from outer coconut husks, are a sustainable option. Because they're packaged in a dehydrated form, the bales are compact and light to carry. While coco coir is a very effective mulch, it's not the best option for an exposed garden as after a long dry spell the chips can become light enough to be blown around by strong winds.

All these natural mulches will break down to enrich your soil and improve its structure so it drains freely yet holds onto valuable moisture.

November is the right time to mulch in many gardens, but it’s important to follow your local conditions when deciding on exact timing, depending on your USDA zone. Applying mulch early might feel like you’re getting ahead, but this can warm the soil too much and delay plants going into dormancy. So, wait until plants are dormant and the ground is beginning to freeze, which typically happens after several hard frosts.

For all the plants that will thank you for the cozy winter coverage mulch provides, a few can be damaged by it. These plants are vulnerable to excessive moisture, poor airflow, or having their crowns and growth points covered so, while they may benefit from a very light layer of mulch, be careful not to smother them.

Winter mulching is all about strategic protection, not simply covering everything in a thick layer of insulation. But get it right and employ a few insulating frost jackets to zip up vulnerable plants and keep them cozy, and your garden will be protected from the worst of the winter cold, ready to flourish once spring arrives.

My 1-year-old cat Daisy has allergies. She is on a special hydrolyzed diet. Iâm trying to find an allergen-neutralizing spray to cut back on dust mites in the house. Would you recommend any specific products?

Since Daisy is already on a hydrolyzed diet, it makes sense to look at environmental allergens too, especially if her allergic signs are continuing. Dust mites are common household allergens, and while the goal is to reduce the amount of allergens in her environment, eliminating them completely is not realistic. Regularly washing bedding and blankets, vacuuming with a HEPA filter, and keeping dust to a minimum are still the best places to start.

If you would like to try a spray, Purefy Anti-Allergen Spray works differently from an insecticide. It is intended to neutralize or remove the allergenic proteins associated with dust mite debris, particularly the proteins found in their feces and other microscopic particles that accumulate in household dust and fabrics. Those proteins, rather than the living mite itself, are an important source of the allergic reaction. So the idea is not to kill every mite in the house, but to reduce the allergen they leave behind.

I would specifically avoid routinely using insecticide or acaricide sprays around Daisy, even when a product is marketed as ânatural.â Cats can be particularly sensitive to certain botanical ingredients and insecticides, including some essential oils and pyrethroids. If you use an anti-allergen spray, follow the label carefully, keep Daisy away from treated surfaces until they are completely dry, ventilate the area well, and never spray it directly on her or on surfaces she is likely to lick. Please ensure you also keep it away from food and water bowls.

Think of the spray as an extra layer of environmental control, not a treatment for Daisy's allergy. The unglamorous combination of washing, HEPA vacuuming, and reducing dust is still doing most of the heavy lifting. And if Daisy continues to have significant allergic signs despite a properly conducted hydrolyzed diet trial and environmental management, it is worth investigating other possible triggers rather than simply reaching for stronger household chemicals. Usually, the answer is not a more powerful spray, but figuring out exactly what is making your cat itchy. So, real detective work is often needed for success.

Itâs that time of year again. Before BublÃ© comes out of his cave and Mariahâs bank balance gets its annual influx, we find ourselves surrounded by candy, costumes, and a plethora of giant orange cucurbits.

Carved into ghoulish jack-oâ-lanterns for Halloween or baked into a delicious Thanksgiving pie, pumpkins have myriad uses, both decorative and delicious, and unlike many festive foods, theyâre also something our dogs can enjoy.

A member of the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae), the pumpkin is a cultivated squash, technically a fruit, with both savory and sweet culinary applications. While some countries wouldnât dare serve a roast dinner without a generous helping beside their potatoes, in the US, the nutritious pumpkin is usually relegated to seasonal decorations or the key ingredient in the eponymous pie.

There are more than 100 varieties of pumpkin with slightly different textures, flavors, and recipe applications. What they all have in common is that they are low in calories, high in antioxidants, rich in vitamins & minerals, and, when prepared correctly, safe for dogs to eat.

Compared with the potato, a vegetable commonly used in both human and canine recipes, the pumpkin is higher in fiber, much lower in carbohydrates, and is far more digestible. It is often included in diets for cats and dogs with digestive problems due to its beneficial impact on intestinal health and function.

Even the seeds of certain pumpkin varieties, when properly prepared, have been found to help eliminate intestinal parasites.1

And the cherry atop this pumpkin pie? Most dogs find the taste of pumpkin irresistible.

Though there are certainly some dogs that challenge this notion, we shouldnât use our dogs as an eco-friendly alternative waste disposal unit. While the occasional table scrap â provided the food is safe for dogs â is unlikely to cause any major catastrophes, offloading ex-display jack-oâ-lanterns and leftover pie is not a good idea.

Yes, pumpkin is a safe and healthy food we can share with dogs, but there are some dos, donâts, and precautions to be aware of.

Pumpkin is a delicious, healthy, and nutritious food that deserves to be seen as more than just a Halloween decoration or pie ingredient. Dogs love the taste, and their digestive systems will thank you.

Give your porch an easy seasonal upgrade with these gorgeous evergreen containers. They make unique festive accents and stunning winter-long living color

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Evergreens are often dismissed as quiet, supporting background players in the garden: solid green shrubs tucked along foundations while flamboyant perennials hog the limelight. Yet when chosen thoughtfully, they can become show-stopping centerpieces. This is a time of year to celebrate the holiday season, but rather than relying on temporary displays, why not go for something with real staying power?

Growing real evergreen plants in containers can provide a brilliant Christmas display that continues looking attractive all winter. Flanking a front door or framing porch steps with holiday porch pots filled with living potted evergreens offers charm and longevity. Beyond classic deep emerald needles, today’s best container evergreens can deliver winter berries, flowers, contrasting textures, and even fragrance to greet guests as they arrive at your stoop.

Best of all, these container-friendly evergreens transition seamlessly from Christmas décor to winter curb appeal that lasts long after the holiday lights come down. With minimal upkeep, they lend easy elegance through the dark days of winter, then you can move them as needed to assist in decades-long displays. From trailing options to compact shrubs, here are 8 gorgeous evergreens you can use to transform your front porch into an enchanting holiday welcome.

Growing evergreens in containers unlocks wonderful design flexibility, allowing you to cluster different heights, trailing textures, and berry accents right at eye level near your doorway. However, while container-grown evergreens are generally easygoing and make great seasonal décor, they need a little more winter care than evergreens growing in the ground.

Because their potted roots sit above ground, they are more vulnerable to freezing temperatures and drying winter winds. It’s a good idea to choose evergreen varieties that are rated at least one or two USDA hardiness zones colder than your local climate, so plant roots have the best shot at surviving winter freezes unscathed.

Use frost-proof containers crafted from thick resin, fiberglass, glazed stoneware, or heavy wood. Avoid unglazed thin terracotta in cold climates, as trapped moisture will expand and crack clay walls. If your winters are very cold, consider wrapping the pots in burlap. Always leave unobstructed drainage holes and elevate your pots slightly on pot feet so icy water doesn't have a chance to pool underneath. You can buy Tortoise Pot Toes from Amazon to help ensure the best drainage.

Fill the containers with a coarse, fast-draining potting mix. Once you are past the holiday season and heading to spring, you can add a slow-release organic fertilizer. Even in winter, evergreens continue losing moisture through their foliage. Check the soil every couple of weeks and water deeply whenever the top two inches (5cm) feel dry and temperatures are above freezing. You’re now ready to add some of these evergreens to make your porch sparkle during Christmas and shine all winter long…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Alberta spruce is a classic choice for a Christmas tree, but most are large. If you fancy flanking your front door with classic, miniature Christmas trees, dwarf Alberta spruce (Picea glauca ‘Conica’) is perfect for a pot. Hardy across zones 3-8, this conifer naturally grows into a dense, velvety green, symmetrical cone, so it requires zero shearing to maintain its crisp silhouette. Also, because it adds just 2-4 inches (5-10cm) of growth per year, it thrives in a generous 14-18-inch (35-45cm) container for years, before needing upsizing or transplanting into the yard.

Place in full sun to light afternoon shade, rotating every few weeks. Keep the potting mix evenly moist but sharply drained, and mist occasionally. For a little extra holiday magic, underplant with trailing wintergreen or variegated ivy. Avoid heavy ornaments that might bend the fine branch tips. You can buy Dwarf Alberta Spruce from Nature Hills at a 30% discount. Add a couple for a lovely, symmetrical entryway feature.

Boxwood (Buxus spp.) brings classic English-garden elegance to winter porches in zones 5-9. Its dense clusters of small, glossy leaves stay green through sub-freezing weather. For containers, choose compact, cold-hardy cultivars such as Green Velvet (which forms a lush, rounded mound) or Green Gem. You can buy Brighter Blooms Green Velvet Boxwood from Walmart. Alternatively, go for pre-trained pyramid and globe topiaries for instant architectural polish.

Place potted boxwoods in partial shade to full sun. In northern zones, shelter them from harsh afternoon winter sun and drying winds. Plant in well-drained potting soil, and water deeply when unfrozen soil dries out. Dress for the holidays with velvet ribbon bows or tuck crimson winterberry stems into the soil around the base. Save any light shaping shears for late spring after the risk of last frost is passed.

Nothing announces the arrival of Christmas quite like holly (Ilex spp.), with its glossy leaves and scarlet berries. While towering tree hollies quickly outgrow porch pots, compact shrub cultivars thrive in containers in zones 5-9. Look for dwarf selections such as Little Red or compact Japanese Helleri. Alternatively, try deciduous winterberry Berry Poppins. Buy Proven Winners Berry Poppins Winterberry Holly from Plant Addicts for a container-sized beauty loaded with vibrant berry clusters.

Just remember that hollies are dioecious. To enjoy berries, you need a female cultivar paired near a compatible male (such as Mr Poppins for winterberry). Failing that, buy a nursery pot where both sexes are planted together. Grow hollies in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic potting mix. Keep berries safely out of reach of pets, and enjoy watching winter songbirds visit as spring approaches.

If your front porch sits beneath a deep overhang or faces north where sun-loving conifers struggle, Japanese skimmia (Skimmia japonica) is a revelation. Hardy in zones 6-8, this neat, mounded broadleaf evergreen thrives in partial to full shade, retaining leathery, aromatic leaves all year. Better still, it delivers multi-season magic: in fall and early winter, male cultivars like Rubella produce clusters of flower buds that last right through Christmas, before opening into fragrant spring blossoms, while female varieties like Reevesiana bear true red berries.

Plant skimmia in an acidic, humus-rich potting mix (such as an ericaceous blend) with sharp drainage. Water regularly during dry spells, using rainwater if your tap water is hard. Nestle pots in a sheltered porch corner that is protected from icy gales. You can buy Skimmia Male Plants from Plant Addicts for shade-loving beauty to bedazzle on a covered porch. Add pinecones and ribbons to make pots festive.

Also known as eastern teaberry or boxberry, American wintergreen (Gaultheria procumbens) is a low-growing native evergreen groundcover. But it punches above its compact 6-inch (15cm) height in winter containers. Hardy in zones 3-8, its shiny, oval leaves transform over winter, from deep green to mahogany-bronze in cold weather. This provides a gorgeous backdrop for large, glossy red berries that cling to the stems all winter long.

Because it trails gracefully over pot rims, it makes a lovely festive spiller around the base of dwarf spruce, boxwood, or winterberry stems in mixed holiday planters. Give it a spot in partial to full shade. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic potting soil. Keep soil consistently damp and avoid lime-heavy fertilizers. You can buy Arbor Day Foundation Store’s Wintergreen Teaberry Pot Plants from Amazon in triple packs. Perfect under a porch cover, awning, or larger tree or shrub.

Goldcrest cypress aka Goldcrest Monterey cypress (Hesperocyparis macrocarpa ‘Goldcrest’) is also sold as lemon cypress, and it lives up to its names in winter porches. Hardy in zones 7-10 (and also enjoyed as a cool-room or sheltered patio container specimen in colder zones), this upright conifer is filled with chartreuse-gold foliage that releases a zesty aroma when you brush past it. You can buy Wonderland Flora’s Lemon Cypress Goldcrest Wilma Plants from Walmart in packs of four.

Its narrow, columnar shape fits neatly into tight entryway corners and pairs symmetrically beside front doors. Grow Goldcrest in full sun to intensify its golden hues, and plant in a fast-draining potting mix. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry, but don’t let roots sit in soggy saucers. Dress the pot base with pinecones and burgundy ribbon for a contemporary holiday look that keeps sparkling into spring.

If you need to soften the edges of a structured winter pot, add some cascading English ivy (Hedera helix). Hardy in zones 4-9, this classic vining evergreen offers lobed emerald or crisp cream-and-gold variegations. Try cultivars like Glacier and Goldchild to brighten shady entryways with ease. While it can be invasive in the ground, it thrives in containers. Plant around the lip of mixed planters with upright boxwood or red-berried skimmia, or train up a wire obelisk for vertical interest.

Ivy thrives in partial to full shade, and prefers slightly drier, well-drained potting soil. Overwatering in winter is the main enemy. Just snip stray runners occasionally to keep trails tidy, and never allow stems to root into surrounding masonry. You can buy Glacier Ivy from Plant Addicts for trailing creams and greens to add lush, lively winter movement.

If you want guests to pause in delight at your front door, plant sweet box (Sarcococca confusa). Hardy in zones 6-9, this understated, slow-growing broadleaf evergreen features dense, pointed leaves that look refined all year. What makes it unique for holiday decorating is that it flowers in winter. Depending on where you garden, you’ll have either buds or open flowers on this evergreen shrub at Christmas time. As a bonus, these creamy flowers are sweetly fragrant even on chilly days.

Sweet box thrives in deep to partial shade and prefers shelter from winds, so a covered front porch or courtyard alcove is ideal. Plant in a medium-sized container filled with rich, well-drained, neutral-to-slightly-acidic potting mix. Keep soil evenly moist when unfrozen. Minimal pruning is required: simply snip a few fragrant sprigs to tuck into holiday vases. You can buy Hirt’s Gardens Sweet & Lo Sweet Box Plants from Amazon for a shade-loving evergreen that fills entryways with honey scent.
